evidence_set: In 11 men abstinent from 7 days to 1.5 years, dopamine transporter binding potential showed no significant correlation with the duration of abstinence in either the caudate/putamen or the nucleus accumbens, while in the same 11 men it correlated negatively with the duration of methamphetamine use (Kendall's tau −0.48, p<0.05, and −0.73, p<0.01). A non-significant rank correlation in 11 people is weak evidence either way. The authors, adding an earlier PET study of people abstinent for more than 3 years, say these findings suggest that a lasting reduction could occur after habitual use.

evidence_set: A previous study (reference 23) using the same PET scanner and tracer found a pronounced striatal dopamine transporter reduction of about 80% in unmedicated patients with Parkinson's disease, against a reduction of roughly 20% in the caudate/putamen of the methamphetamine group here, none of whom had symptoms of parkinsonism or other neurological abnormalities. The authors write that, because striatal dopamine transporter declines with age, people who use methamphetamine chronically may have a greater risk of developing Parkinson's disease as they age, and that in this group, as distinct from Parkinson's disease, the small reduction appears to have predictive value for psychiatric signs.

The abstract says 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine produced peak intoxication (46.0 SD 35.3 versus 30.3 SD 24.9) and drug-liking (47.7 SD 35.1 versus 28.6 SD 24.8) ratings similar to the same dose of d-methamphetamine; the pairs are printed with the d-isomer's value first, so the sentence reads as if the larger value were the l-isomer's. Table II gives the peak means as 46.0 (SD 35.3) for 0.5 mg/kg d-methamphetamine against 30.3 (SD 24.9) for 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine on intoxication and 47.7 (SD 35.1) against 28.6 (SD 24.8) on drug liking, with no mark for a significant difference between them at peak; the Results say few significant differences were found among the peak effects of the active doses other than 0.25 mg/kg l-methamphetamine. In the Results paragraph on ratings across time, the 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine dose produced significantly smaller effects than the same dose of d-methamphetamine on intoxication, any drug effect and drug liking (P<0.0001), and its effects approached baseline at about 3 hours while doses containing d-methamphetamine stayed intoxicating for up to 6 hours.
